extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and responding to obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) determinations during patent examination, including acceptable rationales for obviousness, prior art/analogy rules, applicant reply/rebuttal standards, and evidentiary burdens under 103(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear articulation of reasons for obviousness rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should be made explicit; rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements and must include some articulated reasoning with a rational underpinning (quoting KSR and In re Kahn). Office action should clearly communicate findings and how conclusions are supported by the findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: combining prior art elements for predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results may support a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as an exemplary rationale in KSR; see MPEP §2143 for discussion and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: simple substitution of known elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results may support a conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the exemplary rationales recognized by KSR; evaluate predictability of the substitution and whether it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: use of known technique to improve similar devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the technique was known and whether its application to the similar device would have been predictable to one skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: applying known technique to a device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the device was 'ready for improvement' and whether the improvement would be predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: 'obvious to try' with reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the solutions were finite, identifiable, and predictable and whether a reasonable expectation of success existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: predictable variations from known work across fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects KSR's instruction that design incentives/market forces can prompt predictable cross-field variations; use when variations would have been obvious to try or predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TSM is an acceptable rationale but should not be applied rigidly. KSR recognized TSM as a helpful insight and not inconsistent with Graham. See MPEP §2143 and related discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: TSM may be used but not applied rigidly
rubrics_metrics.description: Although KSR cautioned against an overly rigid application of TSM, it also recognized that TSM was one of a number of valid rationales that could be used to determine obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should use TSM where appropriate but also consider other rationales; explain why TSM (or other rationale) supports the obviousness conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's reply duty under 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references; failure to distinctly and specifically point out errors may render applicant's response substantively inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective traverse requires reasoned statement of error
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings by the Office, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence will not be substantively adequate. Office personnel may repeat the prior rejection and make the next action final if traverse is inadequate (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office consideration of rebuttal evidence (including secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination, including secondary considerations and evidence of unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others; once rebuttal evidence is presented, reconsider the initial determination in view of the entire record and articulate findings of fact supporting the rationale relied upon. See MPEP §§2145, 716-716.10 and cases (Piasecki, Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of rebuttal evidence showing nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may submit evidence or argument to demonstrate that: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods; (B) the elements in combination do not merely perform the same functions they perform separately; or (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office must reconsider obviousness determinations in light of such evidence; examples illustrate how claims to combinations can be rebutted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 is available for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103; admitted prior art can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of statutory categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 103 rejection is based on the appropriate 102 subsection depending on the reference type and dates (e.g., 102(b) bar); applicants may overcome some references by filing affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 to swear behind a reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of the prior art assessed as of the time the invention was made (avoid hindsight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of the prior art is determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight; decisionmaker must 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2145 paragraph X.A for discussion of rebutting hindsight arguments; examiners should avoid using knowledge of the invention to reconstruct obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden to show 35 U.S.C. 103(c) conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant who wants to avail of 35 U.S.C. 103(c) benefits has the burden of establishing that subject matter used in a 103 rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joint research agreement (JRA) protections (post-Dec. 10, 2004), applicant must show: (A) claimed invention made by/on behalf of parties to a JRA in effect on or before the invention date; (B) invention made as a result of activities within the scope of the JRA; (C) application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA. See MPEP §706.02(l).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference must be analogous art to be used in a 103 rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, it must be analogous prior art — either (1) from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem), or (2) reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine analogous art (Bigio, KSR). 'Reasonably pertinent' requires the reference would have 'logically [] have commended itself to an inventor's attention' (In re Icon/Clay). Examiner should consider the problem as reflected in the specification and may include a statement of the examiner's understanding of the problem to support the determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner should consider perceived problem and state reasoning for analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining reasonable pertinence, an examiner should consider the problem faced by the inventor as reflected in the specification and may need to explain why an inventor would have looked to the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem is viewed too narrowly inconsistent with the specification, the scope of available prior art may be improperly limited; applicant's arguments that examiner misconstrued the problem should be fully considered in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give weight to structural and functional similarities when assessing analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: While Patent Office classification and cross-references are some evidence, similarities and differences in structure and function carry far greater weight for determining analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (In re Ellis and others) shows structural/functional overlap can render references reasonably pertinent even if classified differently; analyze structure/function broadly where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider analogous-art principles across arts (chemical/mechanical/electrical/design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy principles apply across disciplines — e.g., chemical arts: teachings across dye chemistry and carriers; mechanical arts: look to areas with similar problems; electrical arts: rate-limiting problems across device types; design arts: general use and designer's knowledge determine analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use art-specific precedents and examples (Ex parte Bland, Stratoflex, Bigio, Medtronic, In re Rosen, etc.) to inform analogous-art determinations; MPEP §1504.03 for design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences must be analyzed with the claimed invention 'as a whole'
rubrics_metrics.description: The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is not whether the differences themselves would have been obvious, but whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim language and consider invention and prior art references as a whole (see MPEP §2111-§2116.01 and cases such as Stratoflex and In re Hirao). Do not ignore unobvious sub-combinations or previously admitted unobvious steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' ignoring claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the 'as a whole' requirement and improperly narrows or alters claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid focusing only on a conceptual gist that omits express claim limitations; cases (W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb) illustrate that disregarding express limitations can lead to improper obviousness findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical prosecution consequences: finality and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should follow MPEP §706.07(a) procedures regarding whether an action may be made final, and review all rejections of record and proposed rejections to confirm continued viability after consideration of applicant submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant's reply is substantively inadequate, examiner may repeat the prior rejection and make next action final; after rebuttal, reassess the entire record and articulate findings supporting any continued rejections.
